concerns.concern_text: The acceptance criteria define latency (<200ms) and throughput (5000 RPS) but do not specify how they will be measured or validated. Missing: test harness type (load test, canary, synthetic), percentile targets (is 200ms p50, p95, p99?), and pass/fail conditions for the gate. Without percentile definitions, the criteria are ambiguous and not reliably testable.

There is no business-level success metric defined. Fraud scoring exists to reduce fraud losses or false-positive rates — neither is mentioned. Acceptance criteria only address operational performance, not whether the service actually improves fraud outcomes. Without a measurable business metric, the project cannot be evaluated as successful post-launch.

No rollback plan is documented in the design artifacts. For a real-time fraud scoring service, a bad model or misconfiguration could cause mass false positives or false negatives affecting transactions. A rollback or fallback scoring procedure (e.g., default-allow, prior model version) must be explicitly documented before proceeding to build.

At 5000 RPS sustained, compute and infrastructure costs could be significant. No cost estimate or cost ceiling is referenced in the design artifacts. This is a required input at the design gate to ensure the project is financially viable before build begins.

With a 5000 RPS throughput requirement and presumably autoscaling infrastructure, there is no documented maximum spend cap. Unexpected traffic spikes or misconfigured scaling policies could result in unbounded cost escalation. A cost ceiling should be defined alongside the scaling design.

agent_responses.reasoning: The design artifacts for RealTime Fraud Scoring v1 establish a focused scope with two operationally measurable acceptance criteria, which is a solid starting point. However, several PM-layer gaps prevent a full approval. Most critically, there is no business success metric — fraud scoring must be tied to fraud reduction rates, false positive rates, or similar business outcomes, not just latency and throughput. The latency/throughput criteria themselves are incomplete without percentile definitions and a specified measurement methodology. The absence of a rollback plan is high-risk for a service that directly influences transaction outcomes. Finally, cost estimates and ceilings are absent, which is a gate-blocking financial governance gap at this stage. I recommend conditional approval contingent on: (1) adding a business KPI as a formal success metric, (2) clarifying latency percentile targets and test methodology, (3) documenting a rollback/fallback procedure, and (4) providing a cost estimate with an autoscaling ceiling.

concerns.concern_text: The design doc and data flow diagram contain no mention of timeout configurations on synchronous calls within the fraud scoring critical path. At 200ms SLA, any unbounded downstream call (feature store, model inference, rule engine) will cause cascading latency breaches and thread pool exhaustion under load.

No circuit breaker or fallback strategy is documented for critical-path dependencies. At 5000 RPS, a single slow or failed downstream service will cause the entire scoring pipeline to degrade. A fallback score or fail-open/fail-closed policy must be defined before implementation begins.

The design does not describe backpressure mechanisms for the 5000 RPS sustained load target. If upstream traffic exceeds processing capacity, there is no documented queue depth limit, load shedding, or rate-limiting strategy to prevent resource exhaustion.

The data flow diagram does not indicate redundancy or multi-instance deployment for any component on the critical scoring path. For a real-time fraud service at this throughput, all stateful and stateless components must have documented HA topology.

No rollback procedure is documented for this release. Given that fraud scoring is likely integrated with payment or authorization flows, a faulty model or rule deployment requires an explicit rollback or model-swap procedure with defined triggers.

The design references handling 5000 RPS with no documented autoscaling cap or compute cost ceiling. Without a maximum instance or spend limit, an unexpected traffic spike or runaway scaling event could produce unbounded infrastructure cost.

Fraud scoring decisions are security-sensitive actions (potential false positives affect legitimate users; false negatives enable fraud). The design does not document audit logging of scoring decisions, model version used, or input feature hashes for post-hoc investigation.

If any third-party enrichment or model-serving vendor is used in the scoring path (not explicitly excluded in the artifacts), their SLA terms must be documented. A vendor with a 99.5% SLA on the critical path mathematically breaks the composite latency and availability targets.

agent_responses.reasoning: The design artifacts establish clear, measurable acceptance criteria (200ms p-latency, 5000 RPS) which is a positive foundation. However, the design is not ready to proceed to implementation without resolving two blocking issues: absence of timeout configuration and circuit breaker/fallback strategy on the synchronous scoring path. At 5000 RPS these are not theoretical risks — they are operational certainties that will cause production incidents. Additionally, high-severity gaps in backpressure, redundancy, and rollback must be addressed before coding begins. Medium concerns around audit logging, cost ceiling, and vendor SLA should be resolved in the final design revision. Recommend conditional approval contingent on a design addendum covering: (1) explicit timeout budgets for each hop in the call chain, (2) circuit breaker topology with fallback score policy, (3) autoscaling caps and backpressure strategy, and (4) rollback runbook outline.

concerns.concern_text: Fraud scoring pipelines typically process high-sensitivity PII (card numbers, account IDs, names, transaction details). The design artifacts contain no mention of log redaction, masking, or scrubbing controls. If PII flows through request/response logging at any tier, this is an immediate compliance violation.

No encryption-at-rest controls are described for any data stores referenced in the data flow diagram. Fraud scoring services ingest financial transaction data which is highly sensitive. All persistent stores (feature store, model store, audit DB) must have encryption-at-rest documented and verified before this gate passes.

Fraud scoring services that receive or process payment card data fall within PCI-DSS scope. The design artifacts contain no PCI scoping assessment, no mention of cardholder data environment (CDE) boundaries, and no tokenization or de-scoping strategy. This must be formally resolved prior to design approval.

Security-sensitive actions such as model updates, scoring threshold changes, and administrative access to fraud decisions are not addressed in the design. A tamper-evident audit log trail is required for financial services compliance (PCI-DSS, GDPR accountability principle). No audit logging architecture is described.

The design does not define IAM roles or permission boundaries for the fraud scoring service's access to upstream data sources and feature stores. Without least-privilege IAM scoping documented at design time, over-permissioned roles are likely to be introduced during implementation. Role definitions with explicit allow-lists must be included in the design.

The data flow diagram does not identify the geographic regions where EU subject transaction data is processed or stored. If any EU resident data is in scope, data residency and processing location must be explicitly documented and controlled before design is approved.

No cross-border data transfer mechanism (SCCs, adequacy decision, BCRs) is documented. Given the global nature of fraud scoring and potential EU data subjects, a legal transfer mechanism must be identified if data crosses jurisdictional boundaries.

The design artifacts make no mention of secrets management strategy (e.g., Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager). Absence of a documented secrets management approach at design stage is a risk indicator for credentials being handled insecurely during implementation.

No log retention or lifecycle policy is described for any log groups produced by the fraud scoring service. Regulatory requirements (GDPR data minimization, PCI-DSS log retention for 12 months) mandate explicit retention policies be defined at design time.

agent_responses.reasoning: The RealTime Fraud Scoring v1 design artifacts present multiple blocking and high-severity security and privacy deficiencies that must be resolved before this gate can pass. The most critical issues are: (1) No PCI-DSS scope assessment despite the service operating on financial transaction data — this is a hard compliance requirement. (2) No encryption-at-rest controls documented for any data stores. (3) No PII redaction or masking strategy for logs, which is an immediate compliance risk. Additionally, the design lacks audit logging architecture, IAM least-privilege definitions, data residency controls for EU data, a secrets management strategy, and log retention policies. The absence of these foundational security controls at design stage indicates the security architecture has not been adequately considered. This gate is blocked pending remediation of all blocking items and documented mitigation plans for high-severity items.

concerns.concern_text: The design targets 5000 RPS sustained with no documented autoscaling cap or maximum compute spend ceiling. At peak or during abuse/attack scenarios, unbounded horizontal scaling could result in runaway infrastructure costs with no guardrail. A hard cap on instance count or spend must be defined before proceeding.

No cost estimate is present in the design artifacts for compute, memory, networking, or ML inference at 5000 RPS sustained throughput. A FinOps gate requires at least a rough order-of-magnitude cost projection with unit economics (cost per scored transaction) before design approval.

The data flow diagram references external data sources and potentially third-party ML model serving or enrichment vendors, but no vendor SLA terms are documented. For a fraud scoring system on a 200ms SLA, any undocumented third-party SLA gap could make the latency target unachievable and expose the business to uncontracted risk.

The data flow diagram shows cross-service data flows but contains no egress cost model. Fraud scoring at 5000 RPS can generate significant inter-region or inter-AZ data transfer volume. Without a documented egress cost projection, total cost of ownership is materially incomplete.

Fraud scoring services frequently process or receive payment card metadata (PANs, BINs, transaction amounts). No PCI DSS scope assessment is documented in the design artifacts. If any card data transits this service, PCI scope must be formally assessed and documented before gate approval.

Fraud scoring decisions are security-sensitive actions (they affect transaction approval/denial and can implicate regulatory obligations). The design artifacts do not document an audit logging strategy for scoring decisions, model version used, or input feature hashes. This is required for regulatory defensibility and dispute resolution.

If EU customer transaction data is processed for fraud scoring, the design must document data residency controls. The current artifacts contain no mention of regional data boundaries, replication policies, or GDPR Article 44 transfer restrictions. This must be resolved before design approval for any EU-facing traffic.

agent_responses.reasoning: This design is blocked at the FinOps/Legal gate on multiple grounds. First and most critically, there is no cost ceiling on autoscaling for a service targeted at 5000 RPS — this represents unbounded financial exposure. Second, no cost estimate exists in the artifacts, which is a mandatory gate requirement. Third, the absence of a PCI scope review is a blocking compliance gap given the nature of fraud scoring services and their proximity to payment card data. Supporting high concerns include: missing vendor SLA documentation for any third-party dependencies on the critical 200ms path; no egress cost model despite high-throughput cross-service data flows; no audit logging strategy for scoring decisions which are security-sensitive and potentially regulated; and no GDPR residency or data transfer mechanism documentation for EU data subjects. The team must address the three blocking items (cost ceiling, cost estimate, PCI scope review) and provide substantive responses to the high-severity items before this design can be approved.
